name: Elena Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers or government, and your answers are confidential. Walk me through a normal shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the loading crew at Cedar Mine and run the excavator when a tricky face needs a steady hand. My two-year technical diploma got me in, but reading fractured rock took years on the job. I use AI every day to sort maintenance notes before the morning briefing. My partner and I have two schoolchildren, a mortgage and a proper savings buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that small AI gains are welcome if we still check the machine ourselves. I already use it to sort fault notes, and it saves me ten minutes before shift. The excavator still needs someone who can read the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and pay look secure in that picture. We have more than six months of expenses saved and other mines nearby. I would still want the fault notes checked because a wrong summary could hide a cracked hose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crew and running difficult loads. I would compare AI summaries against the original fault logs each morning for the first month. If the summaries held up, I would keep using the tool without changing our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little pleased. Ten minutes back at the start of shift is useful, even when the big promises fade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the tool get wrong last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It merged two hose reports that were actually about different excavators. I caught it because I knew the machine numbers. A neat paragraph can still put the wrong truck in a repair bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another tool for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a trial with the maintenance lead. The mine pays for equipment, and I would need proof it saved time without hiding faults. I would not spend crew money for a shiny screen.

I would still trust a **face inspection** over a neat software summary.
think: My **job and pay** look secure, backed by substantial savings and nearby mines.
A wrong **fault summary** could conceal a damaged hose.
do: **Keep** leading the Cedar Mine loading crew and running difficult excavator loads.
**Compare** AI fault summaries with original logs each morning for a month.
feel: **Calm**, with some pleasure in a shorter briefing.
S0.quote: A neat paragraph can still put the wrong truck in a repair bay.
fieldNote: She is a **skilled crew lead** who already uses AI for maintenance notes each day.
Her **cash buffer** and strong local job market make the mild picture comfortable.
She checks original logs because a polished summary can still hide a **machine fault**.

steps.text: Keep leading Cedar Mine loading crew on current shifts
Compare AI fault summaries with original logs each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the planners and buyers will feel this before excavator operators do. The mine should let crew leads test any AI shift plan before it sets load targets. I would offer to run a four-week trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could gain responsibility if I can catch the system’s mistakes, but the office team may shrink. My own seat looks safe while robots spread slowly. I would worry if management treated a faster plan as proof that drivers can skip breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the AI schedule against actual loading times for four weeks. I would ask the dispatcher and two drivers to record delays, then take the results to the mine manager. I would keep my current role while learning the planning screen rather than chasing a new post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for my office colleagues, though I feel reasonably steady about my own income. I do not mind a new tool; I mind a bad target that gets somebody hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What delay would a screen miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rain turns the east ramp slick and slows the trucks. A loading target from yesterday’s dry ramp will fail on today’s rain. I would mark the weather beside every delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would see the trial results?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatcher, drivers and mine manager would all get the same sheet. If the target rose anyway, I would ask for the safety reason in writing. Numbers should travel in both directions.

I would share **trial results** with dispatchers, drivers and management.
think: My **operator income** looks steady while robots enter hands-on work slowly.
Office posts could shrink, and a **faster target** could erode driver breaks.

**Record** wet-ramp delays with drivers and share the sheet with management.
feel: **Uneasy** for office colleagues and about unsafe targets.
S1.quote: A loading target from yesterday’s dry ramp will fail on today’s rain.
fieldNote: She expects **thinking tasks** in planning and buying to change before excavator operation.
Her **pragmatic trial** uses drivers and dispatchers to test scheduling claims against weather and delays.
She remains secure herself, while seeing a **safety risk** in rising targets.

steps.text: Test AI loading schedules against four weeks of actual shifts
Keep leading excavator crew while robots spread slowly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 does not put robot excavators in the pit that year. Capable robots arrive around 2031 in this picture, and the mine would still have to decide whether to buy them. We should test safely and bargain over any lost posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My planning notes could be automated in 2028, but my bucket work lasts until capable robots become available. If the mine buys them around 2031, even a strong crew lead could lose her wage. Our savings cover a long pause, yet two school fees and the mortgage keep me from shrugging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would map which excavator checks need a human and take that list to the safety manager this quarter. In the first year after 2028, I would test AI fault checklists against those physical checks. I would enrol in a paid remote equipment course if the mine posted real supervisory openings. In the first year after 2028 I would keep operating and review the mortgage budget with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I can make a plan, although I cannot promise there will be enough remote posts for the whole crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go on your safety list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ground cracks, loose rock above the bucket and a wrong machine number in a fault log. I would ask drivers to add the hazards they see from their cabs. A robot trial should answer to ground cracks, loose rock and wrong machine numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not before I saw real openings. I have enough savings to take a risk, but paying for a credential with no job attached would be a poor one. I would rather keep that money for the mortgage.

say: I would explain **2028** changes thinking work before capable robot excavators appear around 2031.
I would demand **safe trials** and a plan for any lost posts.
think: My **planning notes** may be automated first, while the excavator seat faces a later threat.

do: **Test** AI fault checklists against physical excavator checks after 2028.
**Enrol** in paid remote equipment training if the mine posts real supervisor openings.
**Keep** operating after 2028 and review mortgage costs with my partner.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan but no guarantee of enough supervisory posts.
S2.quote: A robot trial should answer to ground cracks, loose rock and wrong machine numbers.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking AI** from capable hands-on robots around 2031.
Her course decision depends on **paid training** and posted supervisory openings.
A large buffer helps her plan, but the **mortgage** and possible wage loss keep her anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the longer warning gives the mine time to train crews without rushing. Thinking AI reaches planning by 2031, and capable excavator robots follow around 2034. I would propose a staged trial with drivers and mechanics at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be forty-eight when the planning work changes and about fifty-one when capable robots arrive. That gives me time to build a second skill and pay down more of the mortgage. I still might lose the operator wage if the mine buys robots, so I would not call it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start a remote maintenance diploma next autumn if the mine paid for time off and posted a real job path. I would put a fixed amount from each monthly pay packet toward the mortgage after checking for penalties. I would pilot one AI inspection log with the maintenance team this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less rushed than with the 2028 picture. I can test a new role while I still have a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pilot need to prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every flagged hose would have to match a physical check, and false alarms would be counted too. I would show the maintenance team the misses, not just the wins. A clean dashboard means nothing if the machine stops in the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine does not pay for your diploma?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working and ask nearby mines whether they have funded maintenance posts. I would not quit for an unfunded course while our children are still at school. I can wait for a real offer.

Extra time lets me build a **second skill** and reduce mortgage debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI and roughly thirteen years before capable robots gives a mine time to redesign work fairly. I would ask management to post the training timetable now. We should test robot safety with crews, not in a closed office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives and about fifty-six when capable robots follow. If our mortgage payments hold, we could be nearly clear of the loan, though I would check the figures. I might still want the inspection role, but retirement could also be possible by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the excavator and lead a yearly safety review of AI logs. I would ask the mine to fund younger operators through a technical course before robot trials. At home, I would request pension and mortgage statements before choosing any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own runway, with concern for the younger crew. Thirteen years offers choices that the fast picture does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire as soon as robot excavators became capable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would decide after seeing the pension balance and mortgage statement. I enjoy leading the crew, so leaving early is not automatically a prize. My partner would have a say too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should younger operators get first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time to learn inspection and a chance to work beside experienced mechanics. Young excavator operators need paid time beside experienced mechanics, not just a course. I would put that in a proposal for our next management meeting.

say: I would ask for a **training timetable** during the long warning before capable robots around 2039.
I would test **robot safety** with crews before changing excavator work.
think: At about **fifty-six** in 2039, a smaller mortgage and pension might give me choices.
I would still value **crew leadership** if there were work to do.
do: **Lead** a yearly safety review of AI logs while continuing excavator shifts.
**Propose** paid technical training for younger operators before robot trials.
**Request** pension and mortgage statements before setting a retirement date.
feel: **Calm** about her own runway and concerned for younger operators.
S4.quote: Young excavator operators need paid time beside experienced mechanics, not just a course.
fieldNote: Her own **long runway** and money buffer support a calm assessment of income risk.
She does not assume **retirement** is certain; statements and her partner’s view come first.
She presses for **paid practical training** for younger operators.

steps.text: Keep operating excavator and leading loading crew

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot excavators could follow around 2031, when the mortgage still matters. Paid training tied to posted supervisory jobs would help. I would also want operators involved in safety trials before any crew was cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a crew challenges a machine that gives a confident wrong answer. I have caught a fault note that named the wrong excavator. The new system needs a way for a driver to say stop and be heard.

headlineQuote: The new system needs a way for a driver to say stop and be heard.
portrait: Elena Bauer is a **43-year-old** excavator crew lead at Cedar Mine, with two children, a mortgage and substantial savings.
A technical diploma and years reading **fractured rock** underpin her confidence, while she uses AI daily to sort fault notes.
She tests **AI plans** against real loading times and worries about unsafe targets or hidden machine faults.
Fast robot availability makes her **income uncertain**; longer warning lets her pursue funded maintenance work and examine retirement figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable robot excavators could follow around 2031 while the mortgage remains important.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** tied to posted supervisor jobs and operator involvement in safety trials would help her plan.
